sources.citation: Udoh, Imelda Icheji Lawrence. 2004. Towards Leggbo Orthography. In Ozo-mekuri Ndimele (ed.), Language and Culture in Nigeria: A Festschrift for Okon Essien, 575-586. Aba: National Institute for Nigerian Languages (NINLAN).
sources.note: Sect. 2.3 'Tones': three level tones H, M, L which combine into contours; the three-way contrast holds in noun roots while noun prefixes bear only M or L; verb roots show only a two-way contrast (M-tone verbs vs L-tone verbs whose root surfaces H or L by grammatical context); inflectional tone patterns override (ref. Hyman/Narrog/Paster/Udoh 2002); orthography marks H, L and contours, leaves M unmarked. Nothing on stress or accent. Same content as A's work 2, in an earlier dated publication.

sources.citation: Udoh, Imelda Icheji. 2003. Varieties of the Leggbo Language: A Preliminary Report. In Ozo-mekuri Ndimele (ed.), In the Linguistic Paradise: A Festschrift for E. Nolue Emenanjo, 129-139. Aba: National Institute for Nigerian Languages. [Reissued 2019, Port Harcourt: M & J Grand Orbit Communications; JSTOR chapter doi 10.2307/j.ctvh8qzpb.16; first presented at ACAL 32, Berkeley 2001.]
sources.note: No statement of the tone system or of stress. Contains a first-hand 20-item tone-marked comparative wordlist (numerals 1-10, head, mouth, eye, leg, stomach, hand, finger, teeth, ear, nose) for Leyigha beside Lebamma, Letatama, Lemmabana, Lenyima, Lekuleku and reconstructed Proto-Leggbo (sect. 4.1, pp. 135-136; Leyigha vs PL in 5.1, p. 137), segmental correspondences (4.2), and the sole prosodic remark 'There are also variations in the tones, as in 5.1(2)' (p. 137). Tone marks on the Leyigha forms are wordlist-only data, not a statement. Also notes that previous Leggbo work (Spreda & Spreda 19…

sources.citation: Mbosowo, Sebastian Tom. 1977. An analysis of grammatical errors in the written English compositions of Nigerian students in forms III and V. M.Ed. thesis, University of Alberta. xv+167 leaves.
sources.note: Named only, in a glossary list of 'Cross River 1' / 'Cross River 2 and 3' languages compiled from De Wolf 1971, Greenberg 1963, Talbot 1912, Williamson 1971, Crabb 1965; the thesis is an error analysis of English compositions and contains no description of any Cross River language; nothing on tone or stress.

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry H. 1919-1922. A Comparative Study of the Bantu and Semi-Bantu Languages. 2 vols. Oxford: Clarendon Press. (Semi-Bantu language no. 242b 'Asiga', grouped with 242 Esopong-Arun and 242a Igbo-Imaban; vocabulary taken from Thomas 1914.)
sources.note: Asiga is treated as an aberrant southern member of Johnston's Mbembe (Adun) cluster; only a few forms tagged (242 b) (e.g. Ka-vog 'belly', Wege 'child', E-to 'house', E-bɔijɔ 'ten'); nothing on tone or stress.
